A0008.title: Improving Service Availability
A0008.definition: Improving the number of concurrent terminal requests that can be handled by filtering traffic and increasing server computing resources.
A0008.description: Improving service availability is a systematic engineering effort. On one hand, it requires identifying and blocking malicious traffic; on the other hand, it requires addressing system bottlenecks and improving response efficiency.
A0008.limitation: Cost issues: improving service availability requires significant investment in human, material, and financial resources, which may increase enterprise costs. Technical issues: in some cases, technical limitations may affect service availability — for example, some applications may not be able to seamlessly switch between multiple data centers. Human factors: human factors may also affect service availability, such as human error and malicious attacks.

references.title: Resilience in Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling - AWS

A0008-001.title: Adding Computing Resources
A0008-001.definition: Improving the number of concurrent terminal requests that can be handled by adding server computing resources.
A0008-001.description: For distributed architectures, increasing computing resources is the simplest and most effective way to improve availability. By horizontally scaling or elastically expanding capacity, the system can rapidly increase the number of concurrent terminal requests it can handle, alleviating sudden traffic surges.
A0008-001.limitation: This approach is complementary to business system optimization (A0008-004). While adding computing resources can quickly resolve availability issues, it significantly increases operational costs and cannot fundamentally defend against malicious traffic attacks. Attackers can still exhaust the expanded resources by enlarging their proxy pools or scaling up distributed request volumes.

references.title: Auto Scaling Benefits for Application Architecture - AWS

A0008-002.title: DDoS Protection
A0008-002.definition: Use protected ingress, traffic scrubbing, route diversion, and access controls to identify and filter DDoS traffic while preserving origin availability and legitimate requests.
A0008-002.description: DDoS protection commonly places protected IPs, Anycast capacity, or scrubbing centers in front of a service. BGP diversion sends suspicious traffic through mitigation clusters, where connection rates, protocol features, source reputation, and traffic baselines distinguish attacks from legitimate requests. Volumetric attacks can be handled with scrubbing, blackhole routing, and elastic bandwidth, while SYN floods and UDP reflection can be reduced through connection validation and protocol rate limits. Hiding origin addresses and restricting direct origin access prevents attackers from bypassing the protected edge.
A0008-002.limitation: Large-scale scrubbing and elastic bandwidth are expensive, and blackhole routing also interrupts legitimate access. Application-layer floods that resemble normal requests may bypass edge filtering through residential proxies, low-rate distributed traffic, or direct discovery of the origin address, so cloud bot mitigation, application rate limits, and origin access controls are still required.

references.title: Understanding and Responding to Distributed Denial-of-Service Attacks - CISA

A0008-003.title: Front-End CDN
A0008-003.definition: Configuring a CDN in front of resource access to achieve caching and acceleration of static resources.
A0008-003.description: Dynamic-static separation is a common approach to improve server response efficiency. When dynamic-static separation cannot be implemented or static resource load is high, placing a CDN in front of the origin can effectively relieve server pressure and improve response efficiency.
A0008-003.limitation: Caching acceleration is more noticeable for static resources, while dynamic resources cannot be addressed. Additionally, after CDN node IPs are fixed, attackers may still bypass the caching layer protection by forging source IPs through proxy pools or bypassing CDN back-to-origin routing. Direct back-to-origin connections can penetrate CDN protection.

references.title: What is Amazon CloudFront? - AWS Documentation

A0008-004.title: Business System Optimization
A0008-004.definition: Optimizing the business system to improve response efficiency and reduce resource consumption.
A0008-004.description: Reducing the system load of business requests by streamlining processes, setting up caches, optimizing algorithms, increasing concurrency, and adjusting architecture — thereby reducing response time and increasing request throughput. After optimization, the system can sustain higher concurrency on the same resources, mitigating sudden traffic spikes and resource-exhaustion attacks, serving as a long-term root-cause solution for improving service availability.
A0008-004.limitation: Has a long implementation cycle; suitable for long-term planning but not a quick fix. Requires significant R&D investment.

A0008-005.title: Increasing Business Resources
A0008-005.definition: Addressing resource scarcity to some extent by increasing the available business resources.
A0008-005.description: For example, increasing the quantity of goods, quotas, shifts, or flight schedules can help alleviate resource shortages to some extent by expanding the total allocable business resources, thereby reducing the supply-demand tension after a single point is sold out.
A0008-005.limitation: For certain resources that can yield high returns, it is difficult to directly resolve shortages simply by increasing supply. Malicious actors can still circumvent the added restrictions through methods such as bulk purchasing via proxy pools, multi-account hoarding, and other techniques, thereby monopolizing the incremental resources once again.
